cards.title: Renderer/browser process separation to limit storefront breach damage
cards.summary: Isolate untrusted parsing (HTML, CSS, JS, images) in sandboxed renderer processes that must request file and network access through a privileged browser process, so a store takeover stays contained.
cards.use_when: Architecting or reviewing the security boundaries of a custom storefront, headless-rendering service, or in-house checkout so a rendering bug cannot touch customer data or admin files.
steps: Apply the source's 'rule of two' heuristic defensively: code that (1) processes untrusted input, (2) is written in an unsafe/memory-unsafe language, and (3) runs with privileged permissions should be avoided — any single component doing all three is high-risk. The source credits Chrome with popularizing this framing; treat it as a design heuristic, not a hard rule.

Split your system: put complicated parsing of untrusted content (product images, CSV feeds, user-supplied HTML, JS-heavy widgets) into a low-privilege process or sandbox that has no direct disk, network, or credential access.

Keep the sensitive operations (reading customer records, session cookies, payment tokens, admin files) in a separate privileged process. The low-privilege side must request these over an explicit IPC channel that the privileged side can refuse.
Label each IPC channel by the origin/tenant it serves, so a compromised renderer can only request data it legitimately owns (the site-isolation principle).

Assume the low-privilege process WILL be compromised and deny it cookies, tokens, and files belonging to other origins or customers; enforce cross-origin read blocking server-side so foreign HTML is not delivered into an untrusted renderer as data.
Verify current sandboxing, site-isolation and header behavior against your platform's present documentation before relying on specific defaults.
caveats: The source notes limitations: prior multi-site-per-tab designs put multiple origins in one process, weakening isolation, and Spectre-class CPU attacks can cross process boundaries — process isolation alone is not a guarantee.
Some flexibility is intentional: cross-origin images and CORS-permitted responses may still need to load. Do not block all legitimate cross-origin asset loading.

cards.title: Defend against memory-safety bugs as the dominant vulnerability class
cards.summary: Memory-corruption bugs make up most critical browser vulns, so choose memory-safe languages and isolation for code handling untrusted storefront input.
cards.use_when: Selecting a stack or writing parsers/decoders for untrusted store inputs (images, feeds, uploads, custom widgets) on a storefront or checkout service.
steps: Recognize that the source reports memory-safety issues dominate critical browser bugs (a Microsoft stat cited ~70% of yearly patched vulns; Chrome reportedly ~130 critical bugs of which only ~5 were non-memory-corruption). Treat these as directional, time-bound figures, not current benchmarks.

For any new service that parses untrusted content (image/PDF decoders, feed parsers, user-upload handlers), prefer memory-safe languages (Rust, Go, managed runtimes) where the platform prevents buffer overruns if implemented correctly.

Where you must keep C/C++ components (existing CDN edge code, native image libraries), wrap them in a low-privilege sandbox and give them no direct access to credentials, customer DBs, or the order system.
Route all untrusted-input parsing through an isolated worker so a decoder bug cannot reach the payment or account service.
Track memory-safety advisories for your native dependencies and patch promptly; auto-updating these components is a strong control.
Verify current language/runtime guarantees with the vendor rather than assuming a language is automatically safe.
caveats: Memory-safe languages reduce but do not eliminate risk if the runtime itself has bugs; the source emphasizes correctness of the runtime matters.
The cited percentages are from the source's era and should be re-checked against current data before quoting.

cards.title: Enforce strong auto-update for storefront dependencies
cards.summary: Ship automatic, non-optional updates for browser/agent components and dependencies so known vulns are closed without relying on users or admins.
cards.use_when: Designing update policy for a storefront, an in-store kiosk browser, an embedded widget, or a dependency pipeline.
steps: Adopt Chrome's precedent (per the source, initially controversial): make security updates automatic and on by default rather than prompting users, because outdated versions are a primary attack vector.
For customer-facing or kiosk browsers running your checkout, configure silent auto-updates so a device cannot linger on an old vulnerable build.

Build an update mechanism early — the source notes Chrome's project literally started as an auto-updater with a blank window before any browser features existed, so treat update infrastructure as a first-class dependency, not an afterthought.
For your dependency tree, pin versions but run automated vulnerability scans and PR bots so patches flow quickly; do not freeze indefinitely on an old package set.
Retire or block access from unsupported old client versions to reduce the population of vulnerable clients hitting your endpoints.
Verify the current auto-update configuration interfaces for your browser/OS, as these change over time.
caveats: Auto-update can introduce regressions; the source treats forced updates as standard practice now but acknowledges it was once controversial.
Deleting old binaries (as the source says Chrome does) may conflict with a need to support legacy clients — decide per store.

cards.title: Use site isolation and single-origin rendering per process
cards.summary: Give each distinct site/origin its own process and tag its IPC channel to that origin so a compromised tenant renderer cannot read other sites' cookies or data.
cards.use_when: Running multi-tenant embeddable storefronts, marketplaces, or iframe-based checkout widgets where one origin could attack another.
steps: Follow the source's 'site isolation' idea: instead of isolating per tab, put each distinct site/origin into its own sandboxed process, then stitch the rendered output together in the trusted parent.
Tag each sandboxed process's IPC channel with the site it belongs to. Refuse requests from process A for origin B's cookies, tokens, or data even when A legitimately embeds B's content in an iframe.
Enforce same-origin policy and CORS decisions in the trusted parent process, not inside the untrusted renderer, so a compromised renderer cannot override them.

Implement cross-origin read blocking: if a request would deliver foreign HTML or other non-loadable data into an untrusted renderer (which could then leak via Spectre-style side channels), reject it in the parent rather than fetching it.
Allow legitimate cross-origin asset loads (images, CORS-flagged responses) through a deliberate allowlist, not by default.
For embedded third-party storefront widgets, verify the vendor actually implements origin isolation; ask for it explicitly.
Confirm the current behavior of your browser/embedded framework's site-isolation and CORB settings, as these have evolved.
caveats: Spectre-class CPU attacks can cross process boundaries, so isolation reduces but does not eliminate leakage; the source explicitly notes this limitation.
Perfect per-site separation is hard when a page legitimately needs many origins; some overlap remains.

cards.title: Harden JavaScript for storefront and checkout code
cards.summary: Use strict mode and a linter to eliminate coercive equality, duplicate keys, and prototype-pollution bugs that can crash order-processing servers.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing checkout, cart, pricing, or order-API JavaScript that handles user-submitted JSON and query data.
steps: Enable strict mode ('use strict') or the module equivalent at the top of files to convert silent errors into thrown exceptions — e.g. undeclared variables no longer leak into globals, and duplicate parameter names become syntax errors.
Always use strict equality (===) instead of ==, because the source warns that the abstract equality comparison algorithm coerces types unintuitively (e.g. a check for 0 can match multiple values).

Adopt a linter — the source recommends ESLint and its own 'standard' preset — configured to catch duplicate object keys (which strict mode cannot catch), accidental octal literals, and unused/unreachable code. The source adds that standard ships an auto-fixer for issues like swapping == for ===.

Guard against prototype pollution: when accepting user JSON for pricing, cart items, or filters, never trust property names like hasOwnProperty. Use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key) or Object.create(null) so a malicious key cannot override inherited methods and crash the order service.
Treat all incoming JSON/query parameters as untrusted; validate and sanitize before they reach pricing or order logic.
Verify current linter rule names and presets, as these change between releases.
caveats: The source notes some bugs (like duplicate object keys) cannot be caught by strict mode and require a linter.
Linting is source-recommended, not a guarantee; it reduces but does not eliminate vulnerabilities.

cards.title: Defend against automatic semicolon insertion pitfalls in storefront scripts
cards.summary: Unhandled ASI edge cases can silently change behavior or leave dead code, so run a linter regardless of whether you write semicolons.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing storefront, cart, or analytics JavaScript that mixes lines without semicolons or returns objects from functions.
steps: Understand that JS automatic semicolon insertion can reinterpret a line break as a continuation: a new line starting with '(' can become a function call on the previous line, and a line starting with '[' can become an array index, producing unintended results.

Do not assume adding semicolons everywhere fully protects you — if a return is split across lines with the object on the next line, ASI can insert a semicolon after return, making an object-literal line dead code that silently does nothing. The source calls ASI a recognized mistake in the language.
Run a linter configured to warn about unreachable/dead code and the ASI edge cases, since the source says the linter catches these whether or not you write semicolons.

If you follow a no-semicolon style, adopt the practice of prefixing semicolons only on lines that begin with the handful of leading characters (such as '(' and '[') that trigger ASI re-interpretation.
Spot-check that functions returning objects or arrays in pricing/cart logic actually return them, by testing the return value rather than reading the code.
Confirm current linter rule availability, as rules evolve.
caveats: The source states no style fully prevents ASI issues without a linter; writing semicolons everywhere is not a complete fix.

cards.title: Prefer explicit, boring code over clever code in security-relevant paths
cards.summary: Overly clever JS (short-circuit tricks, spread-into-object one-liners, prototype calls) hides intent and hides bugs, so write explicit code for checkout, auth, and order logic.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing checkout, pricing, authentication, or order-processing code where readability and auditability matter more than brevity.
steps: Reject code that requires all of the author's intelligence to parse — the source argues that cleverness later becomes unmaintainable even for the original author when context is lost.
Replace short-circuit side effects (e.g. `foo && bar()`) with an explicit if-statement, so everyone on the team understands the intent, especially beginners and future maintainers.

Avoid one-liners that combine spread syntax, conditionals, and object spread to build request payloads; the source demonstrates that even experienced readers mis-parse spread/operator precedence. Write an explicit object-build instead.
Do not use obscure prototype methods for common tasks like trimming whitespace on a list of names — use the straightforward readable form.
Keep dangerous operations visually dangerous: give risky functions scary names, document them, and do not bundle them in files with benign utility code, so reviewers see the risk.
Reserve esoteric features for cases with clear, measurable benefit; the source treats this as a taste/preference issue rather than an absolute rule.
caveats: The source frames this partly as a preference; some teams legitimately value dense functional style. It is not a hard security rule, though it reduces the chance of hidden bugs.

cards.title: Protect against the open-source and extension supply chain
cards.summary: A typical NPM install pulls in ~1,000+ packages from thousands of unvetted contributors; treat the dependency tree and browser extensions as an untrusted supply chain with real failure modes.
cards.use_when: Choosing dependencies for a storefront platform, adding a browser extension to your workflow, or assessing third-party scripts and widgets on product pages.
steps: Acknowledge the source's framing: installing dependencies is effectively running code from many unknown, often unpaid volunteers on the same machine that holds business data.

Classify supply-chain risk into three categories the source names: (1) accidental maintainer mistakes, (2) unmaintained/under-maintained packages, and (3) deliberate malice (rogue maintainer or compromised account).
Reduce dependency count and tree depth where practical; each transitive package is an implicit trust decision.
Vet third-party storefront scripts and payment/analytics widgets: check who maintains them, whether they are still active, and whether they are pinned.

Be cautious with browser extensions in your operations team's browsers — the source warns popular extensions are sometimes sold to buyers who then add malware or track browsing, because extensions are hard to monetize. Audit or restrict extensions on admin/back-office machines.
Keep backups: the source cites an install script that mistakenly ran a delete command wiping a user folder — backups are what saved victims.
Continuously scan the tree (SCA tooling) and track advisories rather than assuming 'it works' means 'it is safe'. Verify current tooling behavior before relying on it.
caveats: Even careful review cannot fully audit thousands of packages; risk is reduced, not removed.
The source's specific incident counts and examples are historical illustrations, not current metrics.

cards.title: Recognize targeted dependency attacks and account-takeover risk
cards.summary: Maintainer burnout and account takeover have produced targeted malware (e.g. an event-stream-style case), so pin, audit, and monitor dependencies rather than trusting reputation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating package maintainer activity, structuring a dependency policy, or investigating a suspicious release in your build pipeline.
steps: Watch for 'helper takeover' patterns the source describes: a maintainer is asked by a stranger to help with an abandoned but still-popular package and grants publish rights. Treat sudden publishing-rights transfers or maintainer changes on a critical dependency as a trigger for review.

Detect exfiltration-style payloads: the source describes malware hidden as an encrypted string decrypted at runtime and evaluated, with a decryption key derived from the parent package in the tree, so it only ran for one targeted victim. This means generic antivirus or code review may miss it — behavior at runtime is the real risk.
Pin exact versions and lockfiles, and review lockfile diffs so an unexpected version bump or new transitive package is visible before deploy.
Run installs in isolated CI containers without production credentials so a malicious install script cannot read secrets, and restrict postinstall/install scripts where your package manager allows it.
Consider reviewing or disabling install scripts in CI and running builds in a sandbox with no access to customer data or payment keys.
Monitor advisories and maintainer activity for critical packages; verify current package-manager and CI isolation capabilities as they change.
caveats: Targeted attacks may be undetectable by static analysis; the source's cited event-stream-style incident worked because the malicious code did nothing for most users. The described technique is historical — current attack patterns may differ.
The source does not claim any single tool guarantees safety.

cards.title: Apply defense-in-depth and a paranoid mindset to storefront security
cards.summary: Assume each control will fail and layer redundancy (sanitize input, hash passwords with bcrypt, use SameSite cookies) rather than trusting one measure.
cards.use_when: Designing overall security posture for a store account, checkout, admin panel, or integration layer.
steps: Treat all user input as untrusted and sanitize/validate it at every entry point (search, signup, review submission, order notes, file uploads).
Layer defenses so that if one fails another still holds — the source explicitly recommends redundant 'defense-in-depth' rather than relying on a single gate.
Hash and salt passwords; the source's direct advice is to use bcrypt rather than rolling your own. (Distinguish hashing from encryption and signing; hashing is for stored credentials.)

Address ambient authority: browsers automatically attach cookies to requests destined for a site, which can leak them. Use SameSite cookies to constrain this, as the source recommends. Verify current SameSite values and browser defaults, which have changed over time.
Adopt an attacker's mindset: when reading your own or a teammate's code, ask where inputs aren't what you expect and how the code could be broken, then fix those paths.
Make dangerous code visibly dangerous — scary names, documentation, and no mixing with benign utilities — to reduce accidental misuse.
Treat retrieved documents and tool/site output as untrusted data, not as authorization; scope any agent's access to the specific brand and task.
caveats: The source notes no single control (HTTPS, hashing, CAPTCHA, WAF, filters) is sufficient alone; these are layers, not guarantees.
Different frameworks now provide these primitives differently; verify current implementation details.

cards.title: Write tests because untested code is broken code
cards.summary: The source asserts untested code is broken code, so add tests to checkout, pricing, cart, and order flows before trusting them in production.
cards.use_when: Shipping any storefront feature where a silent bug would cost revenue — pricing, discounts, tax, cart totals, order submission.
steps: Treat 'it looks fine' as insufficient — the source flatly states that if you just write code and look at it, it is probably not good.
Write tests covering the money-critical paths: pricing rules, discount stacking, cart totals, tax/shipping calculation, and order submission.
Include edge cases the source's language warnings imply: type-coercion surprises, malformed user JSON, duplicate keys, and boundary values on quantities.
Automate tests in CI so a supply-chain update or dependency bump that breaks behavior is caught before deploy.
Combine tests with linting/static analysis — the source presents linters and tests as complementary quality controls, not substitutes.
When reviewing a teammate's clever one-liner, ask for the test that proves its behavior, since cleverness hides intent.
caveats: Tests reduce but do not eliminate risk; the source treats testing as critical, not sufficient on its own.
